summary: A note on experiences implementing Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 at several hosts, with the remote host acting as the last intelligent machine before a Computek display. It aims to clarify the coordinate system and puzzles over how to handle text strings. An appendix outlines converting coordinates.

plainLanguage.summary: This note explains how the authors will represent drawing coordinates and keep track of the drawing position while displaying text. It also gives a conversion method for PDP-10 floating-point numbers.

subtitle: Implementers resolve two practical questions about NGP-0 coordinates and text placement.

tldr.problem: NGP-0 leaves unclear whether absolute and relative coordinates use the same number format. The TEXTR command also needs the beam position after drawing text.
tldr.mechanism: The authors choose one two's-complement fraction format for both coordinate types and track the beam position with software X and Y registers.
tldr.outcome: They plan to use this approach in their implementations. The unit metadata says RFC 401 updates this note.

today: The unit metadata says RFC 387 is updated by RFC 401. This note records implementation choices for NGP-0 and does not specify a general-purpose graphics protocol.

sections.title: Implementation Questions
sections.content:
The authors are implementing Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 (NGP-0), defined in RFC 292, at several hosts. They translate it into machine-dependent code for a Computek display and treat the remote host as the last intelligent machine.

This note focuses on two questions: how to interpret coordinate numbers and how to handle the TEXTR command without reading or constantly monitoring the display position.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are adapting a drawing protocol for a display. They explain how they will handle coordinates and text placement.

sections.title: One Format for Coordinates
sections.content:
RFC 292 says coordinates use two's-complement notation, with the leftmost bit as the sign bit, but does not clearly state whether absolute and relative coordinates share a format. The authors compare a format with a narrower range for absolute coordinates against one format that works for both.

They prefer the second format, which represents values from -1 to +1 minus 2 to the power of -15. They say a single format needs less code, handles both coordinate modes, and resembles floating-point mantissas used by many machines. Their implementations will use it for both absolute and relative coordinates.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol leaves room for two ways to store coordinates. The authors choose one format for both kinds because it avoids extra code.

sections.title: Tracking the Beam During Text
sections.content:
The earlier NGP-0 description says a Level 0 command should depend only on that command and the beam position at its start. The interpreter should not need stored modes or stacks. However, the Computek display's TEXTR command must return the beam to the position after the text string.

The display cannot provide a useful cursor reading: input protocols are not yet implemented, and its reading is accurate only to within 4 scope points. The authors therefore keep software X and Y registers. Absolute commands set them, relative commands add to them, both reset to 0 at the beginning and end of a picture, and each character in a text string increments X.
sections.plainLanguage: The display cannot reliably report where the drawing beam is. The program keeps its own X and Y positions and updates them as commands move or draw with the beam.

sections.title: Converting Coordinates for the PDP-10
sections.content:
The appendix describes 16-bit NGP-0 coordinate fractions, with the binary point between bits 0 and 1 and bit 0 as the sign bit. To convert a value to PDP-10 floating point, the implementation moves the sign bit, places the 15 fraction bits at the left of the mantissa, and fills in the exponent.

Positive values use exponent 80 hexadecimal and negative values use 7F hexadecimal. The value -1 is the exception: its mantissa is made the same as -1/2 and its exponent is 7D hexadecimal. The method also works for NGP fractions of up to 24 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix gives steps for converting an NGP-0 coordinate into the PDP-10's number format. The value -1 needs a special case.
